claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and its derivatives are the main techniques used to determine transcription factor binding sites.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and its derivatives are the main techniques used to determine transcription factor binding sites.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific practice in the field of chromatin biology.

claim: Conventional ChIP with sequencing (ChIP-seq) has problems with poor resolution.
source: However, conventional ChIP with sequencing (ChIP-seq) has problems with poor resolution, and newer techniques require significant experimental alterations and complex bioinformatics.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent detailed explanations and comparisons in the manuscript showing resolution differences.

claim: Newer ChIP techniques require significant experimental alterations and complex bioinformatics.
source: However, conventional ChIP with sequencing (ChIP-seq) has problems with poor resolution, and newer techniques require significant experimental alterations and complex bioinformatics.
evidence: This is supported by comparisons to ChIP-exo methodology described later in the manuscript.

claim: X-ChIP-seq was previously used to perform high-resolution mapping of RNA Polymerase II.
source: Previously, we have used a new crosslinking ChIP-seq protocol (X-ChIP-seq) to perform high-resolution mapping of RNA Polymerase II (Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq uses micrococcal nuclease to fragment chromatin and generate precise protein–DNA footprints.
source: By using micrococcal nuclease, which has both endo- and exo-nuclease activity, to fragment the chromatin and thereby generate precise protein–DNA footprints, high-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves single base-pair resolution of transcription factor binding.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach and is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves single base-pair resolution of transcription factor binding.
source: By using micrococcal nuclease, which has both endo- and exo-nuclease activity, to fragment the chromatin and thereby generate precise protein–DNA footprints, high-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves single base-pair resolution of transcription factor binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing to other methods and showing resolution at CTCF binding sites.

claim: X-ChIP-seq requires minimal alteration to the conventional ChIP-seq workflow.
source: A significant advantage of this protocol is the minimal alteration to the conventional ChIP-seq workflow and simple bioinformatic processing.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to other methods like ChIP-exo that require more extensive changes.

claim: X-ChIP-seq requires simple bioinformatic processing.
source: A significant advantage of this protocol is the minimal alteration to the conventional ChIP-seq workflow and simple bioinformatic processing.
evidence: This is supported by statements about using simple thresholding algorithms versus complex peak-calling software.

claim: ChIP was first described 27 years ago.
source: The prevalent technique used in chromatin biology for mapping protein–DNA interactions is chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), but little has changed since it was first described 27 years ago (Solomon et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original ChIP paper.

claim: Sonication is typically used to fragment chromatin in conventional ChIP.
source: For example, sonication is typically used to fragment the chromatin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about conventional ChIP methodology.

claim: Sonication is non-random, with heterochromatic regions showing increased resistance to fragmentation leading to bias.
source: This however, has been shown to be non-random, with heterochromatic regions showing increased resistance to fragmentation leading to bias in the experiment (Teytelman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating sonication bias.

claim: Sonication typically produces chromatin fragments between 200 and 500 bp.
source: In addition, sonication typically produces chromatin fragments between 200 and 500 bp, whereas the footprint of a typical chromatin-associated protein is ∼10-fold smaller, indicating a lack of resolution currently obtained by ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sonication-based ChIP methodology.

claim: The footprint of a typical chromatin-associated protein is approximately 10-fold smaller than 200-500 bp.
source: In addition, sonication typically produces chromatin fragments between 200 and 500 bp, whereas the footprint of a typical chromatin-associated protein is ∼10-fold smaller, indicating a lack of resolution currently obtained by ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about protein-DNA binding footprints.

claim: Extensive sonication only yields fragments with an average length of 200 bp.
source: Even extensive sonication only yields fragments with an average length of 200 bp, suggesting that sonication is of limited use in generating high-resolution maps of genome-wide protein binding (Fan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Sonication is of limited use in generating high-resolution maps of genome-wide protein binding.
source: Even extensive sonication only yields fragments with an average length of 200 bp, suggesting that sonication is of limited use in generating high-resolution maps of genome-wide protein binding (Fan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fragment size limitations and citation to prior work.

claim: Conventional ChIP-seq using sonication yields fragments approximately twice the size of a nucleosome.
source: Answering this question required the precise mapping of PolII with respect to the position of nucleosomes, but conventional ChIP-seq that uses sonication to fragment the chromatin, yields fragments approximately twice the size of a nucleosome.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of nucleosome size (~150 bp) and sonication fragment sizes (200-500 bp).

claim: PolII can crosslink to nearby nucleosomes.
source: Additionally, it has been shown that PolII can crosslink to nearby nucleosomes and therefore mapping the immunoprecipitated DNA fragments from these composite PolII:nucleosome:DNA complexes fails to precisely map the position of PolII on the DNA (Koerber et al., 2009; Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mapping immunoprecipitated DNA fragments from composite PolII:nucleosome:DNA complexes fails to precisely map the position of PolII on the DNA.
source: Additionally, it has been shown that PolII can crosslink to nearby nucleosomes and therefore mapping the immunoprecipitated DNA fragments from these composite PolII:nucleosome:DNA complexes fails to precisely map the position of PolII on the DNA (Koerber et al., 2009; Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and logical inference.

claim: Using MNase to digest unprotected DNA achieves high resolution in ChIP experiments.
source: By using micrococcal nuclease (MNase) to digest unprotected DNA, we were able to achieve high resolution in a ChIP experiment, mapping the precise location of PolII and chromatin remodelers on the DNA (Figure 1A; a detailed protocol is provided as a Supplementary file 1) (Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: MNase-based ChIP can map the precise location of PolII and chromatin remodelers on DNA.
source: By using micrococcal nuclease (MNase) to digest unprotected DNA, we were able to achieve high resolution in a ChIP experiment, mapping the precise location of PolII and chromatin remodelers on the DNA (Figure 1A; a detailed protocol is provided as a Supplementary file 1) (Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: High resolution is especially required at closely spaced transcription factor binding sites such as locus control regions and super-enhancers.
source: High resolution is especially a requirement at closely spaced transcription factor binding sites, such as locus control regions and super-enhancers, which have been shown to be vital to cell fate decisions and human diseases (Hnisz et al., 2013; Pott and Lieb, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on the importance of these regulatory regions.

claim: Locus control regions and super-enhancers have been shown to be vital to cell fate decisions and human diseases.
source: High resolution is especially a requirement at closely spaced transcription factor binding sites, such as locus control regions and super-enhancers, which have been shown to be vital to cell fate decisions and human diseases (Hnisz et al., 2013; Pott and Lieb, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The maximal peak of PolII signal in high-resolution X-ChIP-seq coincides with the position of the polymerase's active site at approximately +35 bp.
source: Using this technique, we find that the maximal peak of PolII signal coincides with the position of the polymerase's active site at ∼+35 bp, as measured by 3′NT.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to 3′NT data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The vast majority of Drosophila genes have a productively engaged PolII enzyme stalled just downstream of the promoter rather than PolII stably bound at the pre-initiation complex.
source: This is consistent with evidence suggesting that the vast majority of Drosophila genes have a productively engaged PolII enzyme stalled just downstream of the promoter rather than PolII stably bound at the pre-initiation complex (Core et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and consistency with the authors' data.

claim: PolII distribution measured by conventional ChIP shows a broader peak centered at the TSS with maximal density at -5 bp.
source: In contrast, PolII distribution as measured by conventional ChIP with the chromatin fragmented by sonication, shows a distinct distribution at the promoter with a broader peak centered at the TSS with maximal density at −5 bp.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B comparing conventional ChIP to X-ChIP-seq.

claim: Accessible regions such as DNase I sites and promoters of active genes are sonicated at higher probability than inactive genomic regions.
source: This discrepancy likely comes from biases in the probability of sonication breaking the DNA at the nucleosome-depleted region of the promoter, as accessible regions such as DNase I sites and promoters of active genes have been shown to be sonicated at higher probability than inactive genomic regions (Teytelman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Analysis of a published sonicated input chromatin sample indicates a strong sonication bias at the promoter region.
source: Analysis of a published sonicated input chromatin sample indicates a strong sonication bias at the promoter region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Using MNase makes it possible to generate footprints corresponding to nucleosomes and other DNA-bound factors.
source: In contrast, by predominantly fragmenting the chromatin with MNase, it is possible to generate footprints corresponding to nucleosomes and other DNA-bound factors (Henikoff et al., 2011; Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves higher resolution than conventional ChIP-seq as indicated by the width of the ChIP peak.
source: In comparison to conventional ChIP-seq, using high-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves both higher resolution, as indicated by the width of the ChIP peak and higher accuracy by avoiding sonication bias, as shown by high similarity to 3′NT.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves higher accuracy than conventional ChIP-seq by avoiding sonication bias.
source: In comparison to conventional ChIP-seq, using high-resolution X-ChIP-seq achieves both higher resolution, as indicated by the width of the ChIP peak and higher accuracy by avoiding sonication bias, as shown by high similarity to 3′NT.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data showing similarity to 3′NT and analysis of sonication bias.

claim: The 3′NT profile was based on 150 million reads.
source: Moreover, the depth of sequencing indicates the cost-effectiveness of this high-resolution ChIP approach, with the 3′NT profile based on 150 million reads (Weber et al., 2014), whereas our method required only 7 million paired-end reads with a fragment length of 20–70 bp.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the 3′NT study.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq required only 7 million paired-end reads with a fragment length of 20-70 bp.
source: Moreover, the depth of sequencing indicates the cost-effectiveness of this high-resolution ChIP approach, with the 3′NT profile based on 150 million reads (Weber et al., 2014), whereas our method required only 7 million paired-end reads with a fragment length of 20–70 bp.
evidence: This is data from the authors' experiments.

claim: The PolII profile generated by conventional ChIP was based on 13 million mapped reads.
source: For comparison, the PolII profile generated by conventional ChIP was based on 13 million mapped reads (Core et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the conventional ChIP study.

claim: A minority of the immunoprecipitated fragments in high-resolution X-ChIP-seq represent the footprint of PolII on DNA.
source: A limitation of high-resolution X-ChIP-seq is that a minority of the immunoprecipitated fragments represent the footprint of PolII on DNA, likely as a consequence of formaldehyde readily forming protein–protein crosslinks generating complexes such as PolII crosslinked to nucleosomes (Koerber et al., 2009; Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data and citations explaining protein-protein crosslinking.

claim: Formaldehyde readily forms protein-protein crosslinks generating complexes such as PolII crosslinked to nucleosomes.
source: A limitation of high-resolution X-ChIP-seq is that a minority of the immunoprecipitated fragments represent the footprint of PolII on DNA, likely as a consequence of formaldehyde readily forming protein–protein crosslinks generating complexes such as PolII crosslinked to nucleosomes (Koerber et al., 2009; Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When mapping murine PolII, only 10% of the fragments were 20-70 bp in length and less than 3% were under 50 bp.
source: In our previous study, mapping murine PolII, only 10% of the fragments were 20–70 bp in length and less than 3% were under 50 bp (Figure 1C) (Skene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is data from the authors' prior study.

claim: Transcription factors typically have a <50-bp footprint.
source: Therefore, to improve the cost-effectiveness of this technique and make it more applicable to transcription factors, which typically have a <50-bp footprint, we have further optimized the method to enrich for short fragments prior to sequencing.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about transcription factor binding footprints.

claim: Agencourt AMpure beads have been used to select for short fragments prior to linker ligation.
source: Previously, Agencourt AMpure beads have been used to select for short fragments prior to linker ligation (Orsi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Agencourt AMpure beads can enrich for DNA fragments below 100 bp from a complex mixture.
source: In agreement, initial attempts indicated that Agencourt AMpure beads could enrich for DNA fragments below 100 bp from a complex mixture, but were unable to selectively purify fragments of ∼50 bp.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Agencourt AMpure beads were unable to selectively purify fragments of approximately 50 bp.
source: In agreement, initial attempts indicated that Agencourt AMpure beads could enrich for DNA fragments below 100 bp from a complex mixture, but were unable to selectively purify fragments of ∼50 bp.

claim: By adjusting the volumetric ratio of beads to DNA, selection can be reproducibly controlled within the 100-200 bp range with a ratio of 1.1×.
source: However, by adjusting the volumetric ratio of beads to DNA, we could reproducibly control the selection within the 100–200 bp range with a ratio of 1.1×, leaving fragments of ∼170 bp in the unbound fraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A 1.1× ratio of AMpure beads to DNA leaves fragments of approximately 170 bp in the unbound fraction.
source: However, by adjusting the volumetric ratio of beads to DNA, we could reproducibly control the selection within the 100–200 bp range with a ratio of 1.1×, leaving fragments of ∼170 bp in the unbound fraction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ligation of Illumina adapters to immunoprecipitated DNA adds approximately 125 bp.
source: Given that the ligation of the Illumina adapters to the immunoprecipitated DNA adds ∼125 bp, by using this ratio of AMpure beads, we could selectively enrich for ligated products containing short inserts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Illumina adapter sizes.

claim: Using a 1.1× ratio of AMpure beads allows selective enrichment for ligated products containing short inserts.
source: Given that the ligation of the Illumina adapters to the immunoprecipitated DNA adds ∼125 bp, by using this ratio of AMpure beads, we could selectively enrich for ligated products containing short inserts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and logical inference.

claim: Using the AMpure size selection approach on input DNA from a MNase ChIP experiment yields a 25-fold enrichment of fragments below 50 bp.
source: Using this approach on input DNA from a MNase ChIP experiment, where the vast majority of the DNA fragments are from mono-nucleosomes, we find a 25-fold enrichment of fragments below 50 bp (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In MNase ChIP experiments, the vast majority of DNA fragments are from mono-nucleosomes.
source: Using this approach on input DNA from a MNase ChIP experiment, where the vast majority of the DNA fragments are from mono-nucleosomes, we find a 25-fold enrichment of fragments below 50 bp (Figure 2C).

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq of CTCF yielded a more focused distribution of reads centered over the CTCF motif compared to conventional ChIP.
source: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq of CTCF yielded a more focused distribution of reads centered over the CTCF motif.

claim: Conventional ChIP using sonication gave a half-height width of 200 bp for CTCF peaks.
source: A conventional ChIP approach using sonication gave a half-height width of 200 bp.

claim: Analysis of 20-50 bp fragments from MNase ChIP gave a half-height width of only 50 bp for CTCF peaks.
source: In contrast, analysis of 20–50 bp fragments from MNase ChIP gave much higher resolution, with a half-height width of only 50 bp, suggesting that genome-wide MNase is chewing back to a minimal footprint of CTCF bound to the DNA.

claim: Genome-wide MNase chews back to a minimal footprint of CTCF bound to the DNA.
source: In contrast, analysis of 20–50 bp fragments from MNase ChIP gave much higher resolution, with a half-height width of only 50 bp, suggesting that genome-wide MNase is chewing back to a minimal footprint of CTCF bound to the DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed fragment sizes and resolution.

claim: Shorter fragments gave the highest resolution and smallest range in peak widths for CTCF ChIP.
source: By analyzing different ranges of fragment lengths, it was possible to see that shorter fragments gave the highest resolution and smallest range in peak widths (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: ChIP-exo is based upon the sonication of crosslinked chromatin, followed by exonuclease digestion of the immunoprecipitated complexes.
source: We also compared our CTCF high-resolution X-ChIP-seq results to CTCF profiles obtained using ChIP-exo, which is based upon the sonication of crosslinked chromatin, followed by exonuclease digestion of the immunoprecipitated complexes (Rhee and Pugh, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the ChIP-exo methodology paper.

claim: In ChIP-exo, sequential ligation reactions allow the demarcation of 5′ and 3′ ends.
source: In ChIP-exo, sequential ligation reactions allow the demarcation of 5′ and 3′ ends and bioinformatic analysis is used to identify 'peak pairs' that flank the transcription factor binding site.
evidence: This describes the ChIP-exo methodology based on established knowledge.

claim: ChIP-exo uses bioinformatic analysis to identify 'peak pairs' that flank the transcription factor binding site.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq is amenable to a very simple thresholding algorithm to identify peaks due to low amounts of noise.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq requires only 13 million paired-end reads to obtain a crisp peak feature for CTCF.
source: Due to the low amounts of noise, high-resolution X-ChIP-seq is amenable to a very simple thresholding algorithm to identify peaks (Kasinathan et al., 2014), requiring only 13 million paired-end reads to obtain a crisp peak feature.

source: This is in contrast to ChIP-exo, where more complex analysis is required, including dedicated software (Rhee and Pugh, 2011; Starick et al., 2015).

claim: For each immunoprecipitated fragment in high-resolution X-ChIP-seq, MNase has chewed back to one side of the minimal sequence motif.

claim: The signal for ChIP-exo is relatively diffuse when centered around the CTCF motif.

claim: ChIP-exo has an average distance of 52 bp between peak pairs for peak-called CTCF sites.

claim: DNase I footprinting is often used to generate maps of global transcription factor binding at nucleotide resolution.

claim: DNase I footprinting has the drawback that the technique is not targeted to a specific transcription factor.

claim: Both DNase I footprinting and high-resolution X-ChIP-seq identify protected fragments with ends separated by 19 bp at the 19 bp consensus CTCF motifs.
source: By comparing the ends of the DNA fragments released by DNase I footprinting and that of high-resolution X-ChIP-seq, we find that both techniques identify protected fragments with ends separated by 19 bp at the 19 bp consensus CTCF motifs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq can achieve single nucleotide resolution.
source: This therefore suggests that high-resolution X-ChIP-seq can achieve single nucleotide resolution, and by using immunoprecipitation, has the advantage that it can be used to interrogate individual transcription factors.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq has the advantage that it can be used to interrogate individual transcription factors.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq has key advantages over conventional ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo in terms of the resolution obtained.
source: By harnessing the endo- and exo-nuclease activity of MNase to fragment chromatin, high-resolution X-ChIP-seq has key advantages over conventional ChIP-seq and ChIP-exo in terms of the resolution obtained (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparative data throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 4.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq is a cost-effective approach for determining precise genome-wide maps of protein-DNA binding.
source: Overall, the combination of the improvements to enrich for short immunoprecipitated fragments and the unparalleled ChIP resolution for PolII and transcription factor binding indicate that high-resolution X-ChIP-seq is a cost-effective and simple approach that easily fits within existing ChIP-seq pipelines for determining precise genome-wide maps of protein–DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by data showing fewer reads required compared to other methods.

claim: High-resolution X-ChIP-seq easily fits within existing ChIP-seq pipelines.
source: Overall, the combination of the improvements to enrich for short immunoprecipitated fragments and the unparalleled ChIP resolution for PolII and transcription factor binding indicate that high-resolution X-ChIP-seq is a cost-effective and simple approach that easily fits within existing ChIP-seq pipelines for determining precise genome-wide maps of protein–DNA binding.
